lesson.title: Snap Decisions: Positive Feedback
lesson.summary: Feeding a fraction of the op-amp's output back to its non-inverting input instead of its inverting input reinforces any change rather than opposing it, driving the output rapidly to one supply rail, which is undesirable for linear amplifiers but exactly what comparators and oscillators need.
lesson.body:
Negative feedback routes a sample of the output back to the inverting input and gets a self-correcting, stable loop. Positive feedback makes one change to that recipe: the sampled output goes back to the non-inverting input, V+, instead. That single change flips the entire character of the loop.

Trace through the logic the same way as before. Suppose the output rises. If a fraction of that rise is fed back to V+, then V+ rises too. But recall from the non-inverting input chapter that a rising V+ pushes the output up further, in the same direction as the original change, reinforcing it rather than opposing it. Each small increase in output produces an even larger push toward more increase. Nothing in the loop settles toward a stable, in-between equilibrium the way it did with negative feedback; instead the output is driven, essentially instantly given the op-amp's huge open-loop gain, all the way to one supply rail, where it stays until something else forces a change. That runaway, self-reinforcing behavior is why positive feedback is called regenerative, and it is also exactly why it is unsuitable for building a linear amplifier: there is no stable intermediate operating point to speak of.

What positive feedback is good for is decisiveness. A comparator built with positive feedback, often called a Schmitt trigger, uses that regenerative snap to switch its output cleanly and quickly between the two supply rails as the input crosses a threshold, without the wavering or chatter that a bare comparator can produce near its trip point when noise is present on a slowly changing input. Work through a concrete design. Suppose the output saturates near +10 V or -10 V (a realistic pair of levels for op-amp rails around +/-12 V once headroom is accounted for), and the feedback network from output to V+ is a divider made of R1 = 1 kilohm from V+ to ground and R2 = 9 kilohms from the output to that same V+ node. When the output sits high at +10 V, the resulting threshold at V+ is Vout x R1/(R1+R2) = 10 x 1000/10000 = 10 x 0.1 = 1 V; the input has to rise above this 1 V threshold to flip the output low. Once the output flips to -10 V, the threshold at V+ recalculates to -10 x 0.1 = -1 V; the input now has to fall below -1 V to flip the output back high. The two thresholds are not the same, they sit 2 V apart (from -1 V to +1 V), a gap called hysteresis, and it is that gap, created entirely by the sign of the feedback, that gives the comparator its noise immunity: a small wiggle on the input near a single fixed threshold could never cause spurious flipping once the trip point itself has already moved 2 V away in the same direction as the last transition.

Positive feedback also underlies oscillator circuits, where the regenerative growth is deliberately encouraged at one particular frequency (using a frequency-selective network like the RLC band-pass filter from earlier in this chapter) and then limited by some form of gain control so the signal settles into a steady, repeating waveform rather than slamming into the rails. Between comparators and oscillators, positive feedback is every bit as useful as negative feedback, it is simply useful for a different job: negative feedback tames gain into something linear and stable, positive feedback is deliberately unstable in exactly the way needed to make a fast, decisive, or self-sustaining circuit.
